slot.brief: System of three equations with a parameter; find the value for which it has infinitely many solutions by checking Δ = 0 and consistency.

stem:
The value of $\lambda$ for which the system of linear equations
$$\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 2 \\
2x + \lambda y + z &= 3 \\
3x + y + \lambda z &= 7
\end{aligned}$$
has infinitely many solutions is:

verdicts.working: Det = λ²−5λ+4 = (λ−1)(λ−4), so singular at λ=1 or 4. At λ=1: eq2−eq1 gives x=1, eq3−eq1 gives 2x=5 → inconsistent (no solution). At λ=4: rank(M)=rank([M|b])=2, solutions x=1−3t, y=t, z=1+2t → infinitely many. Verified numerically.

working:
For the system to have infinitely many solutions, the determinant of the coefficient matrix must be zero:
$$\Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & \lambda & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0$$

Expanding along the first row:
$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta &= 1(\lambda^2 - 1) - 1(2\lambda - 3) + 1(2 - 3\lambda) \\
&= \lambda^2 - 1 - 2\lambda + 3 + 2 - 3\lambda \\
&= \lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 4 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda - 4)
\end{aligned}$$
Thus, $\Delta = 0 \implies \lambda = 1$ or $\lambda = 4$.

Now, test for consistency:

Case 1: $\lambda = 1$
The equations are:
(1) $x + y + z = 2$
(2) $2x + y + z = 3$
(3) $3x + y + z = 7$

Subtracting (1) from (2) gives $x = 1$. Substituting $x = 1$ into (1) gives $y + z = 1$, whereas substituting into (3) gives $y + z = 4$, which is a contradiction. Hence, at $\lambda = 1$, the system is inconsistent (no solution).

Case 2: $\lambda = 4$
The equations are:
(1) $x + y + z = 2$
(2) $2x + 4y + z = 3$
(3) $3x + y + 4z = 7$

Adding equation (2) and equation (3):
$$(2x + 4y + z) + (3x + y + 4z) = 5x + 5y + 5z = 5(x + y + z)$$
The sum of the constants is $3 + 7 = 10 = 5(2)$.
Thus, equation (3) is $5 \times \text{Eq}(1) - \text{Eq}(2)$. Since the planes are not parallel, the system represents the intersection of two distinct planes, which is a line, giving infinitely many solutions.

Therefore, $\lambda = 4$.

Independent check: Det = λ²−5λ+4 = (λ−1)(λ−4), so singular at λ=1 or 4. At λ=1: eq2−eq1 gives x=1, eq3−eq1 gives 2x=5 → inconsistent (no solution). At λ=4: rank(M)=rank([M|b])=2, solutions x=1−3t, y=t, z=1+2t → infinitely many. Verified numerically.
